answers: A North Carolina woman allegedly locked in the trunk of a moving car by her boyfriend was saved by a quick-thinking 911 dispatcher and a lowly flip phone, ABC News reports. The 29-year-old woman called 911 around 4am Jan. 14. The woman had gotten in a fight with her boyfriend, who was "jealous," according to WRAL. Before dispatcher Tim Medlin could get much information from the woman, the call was dropped. He was unable to get her to answer when he called back. Then Medlin remembered a flip phone the 911 communications center keeps around in case the phone lines go down, WTVD reports. He says texting was the only way he could think to contact her without getting "her in trouble." The woman texted Medlin back, letting the dispatcher know she was in a red Mustang headed toward Fayetteville. Verizon provided the location of the woman's phone, and police stopped her and her boyfriend, Nicholas Mattevi, in Fayetteville. Mattevi, 32, was arrested and charged with false imprisonment. "I can go to bed," Medlin recalls feeling upon hearing of the arrest. "We've done our job." He says he's planning to buy a smartphone for the office to replace the old flip phone and make it easier to text if there's a next time. Medlin's boss tells ABC the dispatcher "really stood by our motto: Failure is not an option." (This 911 dispatcher was accused of hanging up on callers.)

full.prediction:
**Summary of News Passages**

On January 14, 2017, a 29-year-old woman in Johnston County, North Carolina, was locked in the trunk of a moving car by her jealous boyfriend, Nicholas Mattevi. The incident occurred around 4 a.m. when the woman called 911, reporting that she had been forced into the trunk of a car traveling on Interstate 40 near the I-95 interchange. The call was initially difficult to understand due to the woman’s distress and was eventually disconnected.

Tim Medlin, a 911 supervisor at the Johnston County Emergency Communications Center, took charge of the situation. Despite multiple failed attempts to call the woman back, Medlin used an old flip phone to text her, a method he had not previously used. The woman responded, confirming that she was in a red Mustang and believed the car was heading toward Fayetteville. 

Using the information provided, Medlin coordinated with the Cumberland County Sheriff’s Office and Verizon Wireless to locate the vehicle. Fayetteville police were dispatched and successfully located the car, rescuing the woman and arresting Mattevi. The woman was found unharmed, and Mattevi was charged with false imprisonment, a misdemeanor. He was released on a $10,000 bond.

The incident highlighted the importance of technology in emergency response. While 911 centers can receive text messages, they cannot initiate them, a limitation that Medlin’s quick thinking helped overcome. Jason Barbour, the director of the Johnston County 911 Communications Center, praised Medlin’s actions, calling it a prime example of using technology to the fullest during a crisis. He also noted that the center plans to upgrade its equipment to include smartphones, allowing dispatchers to initiate text messages in the future.

The event was a relief for the 911 team, who were able to confirm the woman’s safe rescue and the arrest of her abductor. The case underscores the critical role of emergency dispatchers in saving lives and preventing serious crimes, even in the face of technological limitations.
